open-question.question: Where should the macOS build script live, and what should it be called? The repo has no scripts/ directory or app build script yet. Options include a repo-root scripts/build-macos.sh, a script inside flutter/, or something else.
open-question.alternative: Create a new top-level `scripts/` directory and put the script there as `scripts/build-macos.sh`. It resolves the repo root from its own location, then runs `mopro build` at the root and `flutter build macos` inside `flutter/`. This starts a repo-level convention in a repo that has none yet. A future `scripts/build-linux.sh` or a Windows/WSL script fits beside it with matching names. The script also sits at the level where its first step (`mopro build`, driven by the root `Config.toml`) runs and where the three version files it compares (`Cargo.toml`, `flutter/pubspec.yaml`, `mopro_flutter_bindings/rust/Cargo.toml`) are equally reachable. It adds a new top-level directory holding a single file. The generic "build" name also hides the fact that the script signs and packages a dmg as well as building. That may be a problem next to future scripts, unless those scripts follow the same build-plus-package pattern.

Put the script in the Flutter project, as `flutter/build-macos.sh` or `flutter/scripts/build-macos.sh`, so it lives next to `flutter/macos/` and the `flutter build` it runs. It sits beside the app it packages, where `Release.entitlements`, `AppInfo.xcconfig` and `flutter/build/macos/Build/Products/Release` are. It also matches the "Build from Source" section of `docs/Linux.md`, which already tells people to `cd flutter` before building. The script's first step, `mopro build`, has to run from the repo root and regenerates the `mopro_flutter_bindings/` bindings, and it checks `Cargo.toml` versions outside `flutter/`. So a script inside `flutter/` has to climb out of its own directory for its main work, which makes it look narrower than it is. It also places a repo-wide release tool inside a subproject whose `build/` directory is git-ignored and removed by `flutter clean`, which makes a misplaced path an easy mistake.

Put the script directly in the repo root, next to `Cargo.toml` and `Config.toml`, with a name that says what it produces, e.g. `build-macos-dmg.sh` or `release-macos.sh`. It is the easiest place to find: it shows up with `ls` next to the README, it needs no new directory, and it follows the pattern the repo already has of a runnable `.sh` at the top level of the tree it works on (e.g. `groth16-prover-min/build-circuit.sh`, `claim-relayer/e2e-anvil/run.sh`). A name like `build-macos-dmg.sh` also states the output clearly. It clutters a root that already holds the mopro crate files (`build.rs`, `Config.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), where a stray shell script can look like part of the Rust/mopro build. It also sets no pattern for more platform scripts, so a later Linux or Windows packaging script would either pile up at the root or force a move to `scripts/`.

open-question.question: Where should the script write the final .dmg and its intermediate staging files? For example, a git-ignored dist/ directory at the repo root, or somewhere under flutter/build/. Should an existing output be overwritten or should the script refuse?
open-question.alternative: Write the final dmg to a new `dist/` directory at the repo root, and add a new `dist/` entry to the root `.gitignore` because nothing ignores it today. Build the dmg staging folder (the `.app` copy and the `/Applications` symlink) in a `mktemp -d` directory that is deleted by an exit `trap`. Silently replace any existing dmg of the same name. The output is easy to find and separate from all build state. A `flutter clean` or removing `flutter/build/` never deletes a finished release dmg. Staging in a temp directory means a failed run leaves no half-built staging tree behind. Re-running for the same version just works, which suits a build → sign → dmg dry run repeated until it passes. It adds a new top-level directory and a `.gitignore` change. Silent overwrite can replace a dmg whose SHA-256 was already published on a GitHub release. If the same version is rebuilt, the new file's checksum will differ from the published one, and nothing warns about it.

Use the same git-ignored repo-root `dist/` for the final dmg and a temp directory for staging. If the target dmg already exists, the script stops with an error before doing any build work, unless a flag such as `--force` is passed to allow overwriting. A dmg whose checksum may already be on a GitHub release is never replaced by accident. The versioned file name makes a name clash mean exactly "this version was already packaged", so refusing is a meaningful safeguard. Checking up front also avoids wasting a long `mopro build` / `flutter build macos` run. It adds a flag and a code path to the script. Repeated dry runs of the same version need `--force` or a manual delete every time, which gets in the way during this milestone's fix-until-it-passes loop. How often this bites depends on how the version-naming question settles.

Put both the staging folder and the final dmg under the Flutter build tree, for example `flutter/build/macos/dmg/`, next to the `Build/Products/Release` app it packages. Replace existing output freely because it is a disposable build product. It needs no new directory and no `.gitignore` change, because the root and `flutter/.gitignore` `build/` patterns already cover it. It keeps every artifact of one build in one place, next to the `.app` it came from. The dmg is hidden deep in a build tree, and it is lost whenever that tree is wiped. `flutter clean` deletes all of `flutter/build/`, so if the clean-build policy runs a clean at the start of each build, the previous release dmg disappears without warning. Nothing marks it apart from the intermediate files.

Write both staging and the final dmg to a directory under a repo-root `build/`, for example `build/macos/`, which the root `.gitignore`'s existing `build/` pattern already ignores. Replace existing output on each run. The output sits at the top level where it is easy to find. It needs no `.gitignore` edit. It is outside the Flutter project, so `flutter clean` does not touch it. A root `build/` next to cargo's `target/` suggests an intermediate build tree rather than a release deliverable. Keeping staging and the final dmg in the same place makes it easier to confuse or accidentally delete the finished artifact. Silent overwrite has the same risk of changing an already-published checksum.

open-question.question: Which file is the authoritative version for the dmg file name and the bundle's CFBundleShortVersionString? Candidates are the root Cargo.toml (currently 0.5.1) and flutter/pubspec.yaml (currently 0.5.0). What should the script do when they disagree, given that it only warns?
open-question.alternative: The script reads the version from flutter/pubspec.yaml (currently 0.5.0) and uses it for the dmg file name. It runs flutter build macos without overriding the version, so CFBundleShortVersionString comes from FLUTTER_BUILD_NAME as Info.plist already does. If the root Cargo.toml or the bindings dependency disagrees, the script prints a warning naming both values and carries on. No build flags are needed, and the name and bundle always agree. The dmg name, the About/Finder version and the pubspec are the same value because Flutter already takes it from the pubspec. With the repo as it is, the first build is 0.5.0 even though the latest tag is v0.5.1 and Cargo.toml says 0.5.1. Unless the pubspec is bumped first, the release is published under an older version than it contains. Fixing that mismatch is out of scope for this milestone.

The script reads the version from the root Cargo.toml (currently 0.5.1, which matches the latest tag and the bindings dependency). It uses that version for the dmg name and passes it to flutter build macos --build-name, so it overrides the pubspec in CFBundleShortVersionString. If pubspec.yaml disagrees, the script warns and says the pubspec value was overridden. With the repo as it is, this gives the correct 0.5.1 in both the file name and the bundle. It also follows the two files CLAUDE.md already requires to match (the root Cargo.toml and the bindings dependency), with no need to fix the pubspec first. The bundle's version no longer comes from the pubspec, so a plain flutter build macos made by hand gives a different CFBundleShortVersionString than the script does. Anyone who bumps only the pubspec later is quietly overridden, and a warning is the only sign.

The maintainer passes the release version on the command line, or the script takes it from the git tag at HEAD (for example v0.5.1 without the "v"). The script uses it for the dmg name and passes it as --build-name. It checks it against Cargo.toml, the bindings dependency and pubspec.yaml, and warns about each file that differs. The version stays tied to the release tag being published instead of to either file, so the mismatch neither file can settle on its own does not choose the name. Every file that disagrees is reported the same way. It adds a required input or a dependency on the git state. A build without a tag or without the argument needs a fallback rule, which brings back the question of which file wins. The bundle version can also differ from both files, which is confusing when someone looks at the build later.

open-question.question: What exact naming convention should the dmg file and its mounted volume use? The Linux release uses zkp-migration-app-linux-amd64.tar.gz with no version. Should the macOS file follow the same pattern with a version added (e.g. zkp-migration-app-macos-arm64-<version>.dmg)? What volume name should users see when they open it?
open-question.alternative: Name the file `zkp-migration-app-macos-arm64-<version>.dmg`. This follows the Linux `zkp-migration-app-linux-amd64.tar.gz` stem, swaps in the macOS platform and arch, and puts the version at the end. Set the volume name to the bundle's product name, `Zero Knowledge Migration App`, with no version. It matches the only existing release artifact name almost exactly. Users and the release page see one consistent family of names, and the lowercase, hyphenated file name has no spaces, so the `shasum -a 256` command in docs/macOS.md needs no quoting. The volume shows the same name as the `.app` users drag to `/Applications`, which is what Finder users expect. The version comes after the platform and arch, so a sorted list of files from several releases groups by platform rather than by release. Because the volume name has no version, two mounted dmgs from different releases look the same in Finder. The Linux artifact still has no version, so the two platforms' names stay inconsistent unless the Linux name is changed later, which this milestone does not cover.

Name the file `zkp-migration-app-<version>-macos-arm64.dmg`, or with the git-tag form `zkp-migration-app-v<version>-macos-arm64.dmg` so it matches tags like `v0.5.1`. Set the volume name to include the version, e.g. `Zero Knowledge Migration App <version>`. This follows the common `name-version-platform-arch` convention used by many projects' GitHub release assets. Files from several releases sort by release, the name ties directly to the git tag the release comes from, and the versioned volume name shows users which release they have mounted. It departs from the Linux artifact's `name-platform-arch` order, so the release page mixes two naming schemes. The `v` prefix, if used, is one more format detail the script must derive and keep consistent. A versioned volume name also has spaces and changes every release, so any doc step or script test-mount that refers to `/Volumes/<name>` has to be versioned as well.

Name the file after the app's display name, e.g. `Zero Knowledge Migration App-<version>-arm64.dmg` (or a space-free variant such as `ZeroKnowledgeMigrationApp-<version>-arm64.dmg`). Set the volume name to `Zero Knowledge Migration App`, as many native macOS apps do. What users download, what they see mounted, and what lands in `/Applications` all carry the same human-readable product name. That makes the download easy to recognise for non-technical macOS users following docs/macOS.md. It shares nothing with the `zkp-migration-app-*` Linux name, so release assets no longer form one recognisable family. The spaced form also needs quoting in every `shasum`, `hdiutil` and `codesign` command in the script and the user doc, and it gets URL-encoded in GitHub release download links.

open-question.question: Xcode already ad-hoc signs the Release build with Release.entitlements (app-sandbox and network.client), but codesign --force --deep -s - without --entitlements removes them. Should the script re-sign explicitly with flutter/macos/Runner/Release.entitlements, keep Xcode's signature and only verify it, or do something else? Should the app stay sandboxed?
open-question.alternative: The script keeps the goal's ad-hoc re-sign step but passes the entitlements file explicitly: `codesign --force --deep -s - --entitlements flutter/macos/Runner/Release.entitlements` on the app bundle. The app stays sandboxed with `app-sandbox` and `network.client`, the same configuration Xcode applies. It follows the goal's stated `codesign --force --deep -s -` step and still ships the same sandbox and network entitlements the project already declares for Release. The file in git stays the single source of truth for entitlements, and the zkey keeps its home under `~/Library/Containers/com.zilliqa.zkpRecoveryApp/`. With `--deep`, the app's entitlements are also stamped onto the embedded frameworks (FlutterMacOS, App, the Rust pod). Apple discourages `--deep` for signing. Keeping it clean means signing nested code first without entitlements and then signing the outer app with them, which makes the script longer. The sandbox also has to be confirmed at runtime, because the zkey download and file access have only been checked in Debug.

The script skips re-signing and ships the ad-hoc signature `flutter build macos` already produces (`CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY = "-"` with Release.entitlements). It only runs `codesign --verify --deep --strict` and checks that the expected entitlements are present. Nothing is signed twice, so the entitlements cannot be lost by accident and there is no `--deep` signing. The shipped signature is exactly what Xcode's project settings define, which makes this the simplest and least error-prone path. It departs from the goal's explicit `codesign --force --deep -s -` step, so the goal text would need to change. It also depends on Xcode signing every nested framework and dylib correctly (including the cargokit-built Rust library). If any of them come out unsigned or with a mismatched signature, the script can only report the failure, not fix it.

The script runs the plain `codesign --force --deep -s -` from the goal with no entitlements, so the app ships unsandboxed. Release.entitlements would ideally be changed to match, so the Xcode build and the shipped app don't differ. It is the simplest signing step and matches the goal's command word for word. An ad-hoc app without the hardened runtime or a sandbox needs no entitlements to reach the network or write files. Container path differences go away, and the app behaves like the Linux and Windows builds. It drops OS-level isolation for an app that handles BIP-39 mnemonics, which is a real step down in security. The zkey moves from the sandbox container to `~/Library/Application Support/com.zilliqa.zkpRecoveryApp/`. And unless Release.entitlements is edited too, the shipped app quietly differs from what the Xcode project declares.

open-question.question: Should the script always run mopro build (which regenerates the committed Dart bindings and can leave the working tree dirty), make it optional with a flag, or skip it by default? If mopro-cli is missing, should the script just fail with install instructions or install it automatically?
open-question.alternative: The script always runs `mopro build` before `flutter build macos`. If `mopro` is not on PATH, it stops straight away and prints the install command (`cargo install mopro-cli`). If the committed bindings under `mopro_flutter_bindings/lib/src/rust/` change, it reports that with a `git status`/`git diff --stat` notice after the step. This matches the milestone Goal as written ("runs `mopro build` and `flutter build macos`"). Every dmg is built from bindings freshly regenerated from the current Rust API and circuit, so a stale-bindings release can't happen. The script also never changes the machine's toolchain without the maintainer knowing. Every run needs mopro-cli, which is not installed on the developer machine today. `mopro build` also adds a full release Rust compile on top of the one cargokit already does during `flutter build macos`. A regeneration can leave committed generated files dirty, for example from a different mopro-cli or flutter_rust_bridge version than the one that produced the frb 2.11.1 bindings. Whether that is only reported or blocks the build depends on how the clean-working-tree prerequisite is settled.

The script always runs `mopro build`. If `mopro` is missing, it installs mopro-cli itself with `cargo install mopro-cli`, ideally pinned with `--version`/`--locked` to a release compatible with the crate's `mopro-ffi =0.3.7`, and then continues. A new maintainer machine goes from checkout to dmg with one command and no manual setup. That would have covered the one gap found on this machine, where mopro was missing. The build script changes the maintainer's global cargo install, and a first run takes a long time. Unless the version is pinned and kept current by hand, `cargo install mopro-cli` picks up the latest CLI, which may generate bindings that don't match the committed ones or the pinned `mopro-ffi =0.3.7`/frb 2.11.1. That puts an unreviewed toolchain change into the release artifact.

`mopro build` runs by default. An opt-out flag (e.g. `--skip-mopro`) builds straight from the committed bindings. mopro-cli is only required, and a missing one only fails the run with install instructions, when the step isn't skipped. The Goal's default behaviour and its freshness guarantee stay the same. Maintainers who know the Rust API and circuit haven't changed can skip the extra Rust compile and the dirty-tree churn, and a machine without mopro can still build. Two build paths need documenting and testing. Also, the skip is chosen by the maintainer rather than detected, so a release can still ship with stale bindings if someone uses the flag after a Rust API change.

By default the script builds from the committed Dart bindings and relies on cargokit's pod "Build Rust library" phase to compile the native library during `flutter build macos`. `mopro build` runs only with an opt-in flag (e.g. `--regen-bindings`), and mopro-cli is checked (fail with instructions) only in that case. The release build treats the committed bindings as the source of truth and never dirties the working tree. It doesn't need mopro-cli at all, and it skips a redundant release Rust compile, since the native library is built by cargokit either way. Regenerating bindings stays a deliberate step that gets committed, not a side effect of packaging. This goes against the Goal as written, which lists `mopro build` as a step the script runs, so choosing it means amending the Goal. It also relies on the committed bindings actually matching the Rust API. If someone changes the Rust API or circuit and forgets to run `mopro build` and commit, the mismatch only shows up as a build or runtime failure instead of being regenerated automatically.

open-question.question: Which prerequisites should the script check before building, and how strict should each check be? Candidates: host is arm64 macOS, Xcode command-line tools, flutter, CocoaPods, cargo/rustup with the aarch64-apple-darwin target, mopro, hdiutil/codesign/shasum, a clean git working tree, and building on a release tag or branch. Which of these fail the build and which only warn?
open-question.alternative: Tool checks fail, git checks warn. Before building, the script fails with an install hint for each missing tool that has no workaround. That covers an arm64 macOS host (`uname -s`/`uname -m`), the Xcode command-line tools (`xcode-select -p`), `flutter`, CocoaPods `pod`, `cargo`/`rustup` with `aarch64-apple-darwin` in `rustup target list --installed`, and `hdiutil`/`codesign`/`shasum`. A dirty working tree or a HEAD that is not a release tag or `release/*` branch only prints a warning. The `mopro` check follows whatever the mopro-handling decision says: it fails only if `mopro build` is going to run. Every toolchain gap shows up in the first seconds with a clear fix, not deep inside a long `mopro build`/`flutter build macos`/cargokit run. The script still works for this milestone's dry run, which happens on the feature branch `user/lukasz/macos_dist` with a tree that `mopro build` may itself dirty. It also matches the Goal's existing pattern of warning without stopping, as for the version mismatch. Nothing stops a maintainer from publishing a dmg built from uncommitted or untagged code. The warning is easy to scroll past, so the dmg on the GitHub release may not match any commit, and whether it is reproducible depends on the maintainer's discipline.

Everything fails, with explicit overrides. Every candidate check fails the build, including the git checks: a dirty working tree fails and so does a HEAD that is not a release tag or `release/*` branch. Flags like `--allow-dirty` and `--allow-untagged` (or one `--dev` flag) turn the git failures into warnings. The clean-tree check runs before `mopro build`, so regenerated bindings are not counted against it. By default, any artifact that could be released comes from a committed, tagged state, so the published SHA-256 can be traced to a specific commit. Skipping that guarantee takes a deliberate flag that anyone can see. The milestone's own dry run on a feature branch cannot pass without the override flags, and so will every day-to-day test build. This adds flag handling and documentation for a solo developer-machine workflow. If regenerated bindings are expected to be committed as part of the release, the clean-tree rule can also clash with `mopro build` dirtying the tree.

Minimal presence checks. The script fails only if the host is not arm64 macOS or a command it calls directly is missing from `PATH` (`command -v` for `flutter`, `pod`, `cargo`, `hdiutil`, `codesign` and `shasum`, plus `mopro` if it runs). It does not check the Xcode tools setup or the installed Rust target, and it does not check git state. Deeper problems are left to `flutter build macos`, CocoaPods and cargokit to report. It is the smallest and least brittle script. It does not try to reproduce checks the underlying tools already do, and it will not falsely fail on some other valid way of installing rustup/Xcode. Some problems only show up after minutes of building, as cryptic cargokit or Xcode errors, for example a missing `aarch64-apple-darwin` target or the command-line tools pointing to the wrong Xcode. The script also says nothing about dirty or untagged release builds.

open-question.question: Should the script always start from a clean build (e.g. flutter clean and removing the previous Release products) so release artifacts are reproducible? Or should it reuse incremental build state for speed, perhaps with a flag to choose?
open-question.alternative: The script always starts with `flutter clean` and deletes any earlier Release products and staging output. No incremental state carries over into a release dmg. Every dmg is built from the checked-out sources and nothing else. A leftover Debug build (the only thing now under `flutter/build/macos/Build/Products/`), stale pods, or a stale cargokit Rust library can't slip into a release, so the published SHA-256 always comes from the same kind of build. Every run is slow. `flutter/build` is about 2.2 GB, and cargokit's Rust output sits in Xcode's `TARGET_TEMP_DIR` inside it. Cleaning therefore forces a full recompile of the Arkworks/circom-prover crate, including the `rust_witness` transpile of the ~679k-constraint `groth.wasm`, on every attempt. That hurts most while the milestone's dry run is being fixed. Also, a clean build is not byte-reproducible anyway, because timestamps and ad-hoc signatures still vary.

By default the script reuses the existing Flutter, pod and cargokit build state. A `--clean` flag runs `flutter clean` and removes the earlier Release products before building. Quick iteration while developing and debugging the script, since repeated runs skip the long Rust rebuild. A clean release build is still one flag away. A maintainer can forget the flag, and the default path is the less trustworthy one. A dmg built on stale state, such as bindings or a Rust library from before a `mopro build` or version bump, looks just like a clean one. Nothing records whether a published artifact was built clean.

By default the script cleans the Flutter build and earlier Release products. An opt-in flag such as `--incremental` or `--no-clean` skips the clean so a developer can iterate quickly. The default is the safe one for release artifacts, and a fast path is still there for script development and repeated dry runs. The warning could mark incremental builds, for example in output or dmg naming, so they aren't mistaken for release builds. There are two code paths to maintain and document. Anyone who habitually passes the fast flag loses the guarantee without noticing, unless the script clearly labels incremental output as not for release.

The script never runs a full `flutter clean`. Instead it always deletes only the outputs that decide what gets shipped: the Release `.app` under `flutter/build/macos/Build/Products/Release/` and the dmg staging directory. Xcode, pod and cargokit compile caches are left for Flutter and Xcode's own dependency tracking to invalidate. Most of the benefit at little cost. A stale or leftover app bundle can never be packaged, because the bundle that gets signed and put in the dmg is always freshly produced by this run's `flutter build macos`. The expensive Rust compile cache is kept. It relies on Xcode and cargokit invalidating their caches correctly, for example after the bindings are regenerated or the pubspec version changes. Any mistake in that dependency tracking ends up in the release unnoticed. It also differs from a truly clean build if the machine's toolchain or pods change between runs.

open-question.question: Which checks should the script run after building, and what counts as success? For example: codesign --verify --deep --strict on the app, checking the entitlements are present, hdiutil verify on the dmg, a test mount, and spctl --assess. spctl is expected to reject an ad-hoc-signed app, so should it be reported for information only?
open-question.alternative: The script fails the build only if `codesign --verify --deep --strict` fails on the built `Zero Knowledge Migration App.app` or `hdiutil verify` fails on the finished dmg. It does not check entitlements and does not mount the dmg. It leaves `spctl --assess` out, or at most prints its expected rejection with an "informational" label and never lets it change the exit status. Only two checks can fail, and both are reliable system-tool results. The script stays short, and the dry run can pass without any environment-specific test mounts or output that is hard to read. A signature can be valid and still be missing the `app-sandbox` and `network.client` entitlements, since `codesign --force --deep -s -` without `--entitlements` drops them silently. This gate would not catch that, or a dmg missing the app or the `/Applications` shortcut. Those problems would only show up in the later manual launch test. How much the entitlement gap matters depends on how the entitlements question is settled.

After building, the script runs several checks, and any failure stops it with a non-zero exit. The checks are: - `codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=2` on the app. - `codesign -d --entitlements -` compared with the expected set in `flutter/macos/Runner/Release.entitlements`. - `hdiutil verify` on the dmg. - A read-only, no-browse test mount (`hdiutil attach -readonly -nobrowse`). It confirms the `.app` and the `/Applications` symlink are present, re-runs `codesign --verify` on the mounted copy, and then detaches in a trap. `spctl --assess --type execute` is run last. Its expected rejection of an ad-hoc signature is printed as information and never fails the run. It catches each way the pipeline is likely to break: lost entitlements after re-signing, a dmg that is corrupt or missing its contents, and a signature damaged by the copy into the image. The dry-run success criterion then covers the whole build → sign → dmg chain, not just the two tools' exit codes. It adds more code that has to be right, including a mount/detach trap and entitlement comparison against plist or XML output. The entitlement comparison assumes a known expected set, so if the entitlements question settles on something other than the current `Release.entitlements`, this check has to be changed to match. A leftover mount from an interrupted run can also make later runs fail.

This runs every check in the layered gate above. It also fails on these bundle-content checks: - `lipo -archs` on the main executable and on the bundled frameworks must report `arm64`, and this milestone ships an arm64-only build. - `Info.plist` `CFBundleIdentifier` must be `com.zilliqa.zkpRecoveryApp`. - `Info.plist` `CFBundleShortVersionString` must match the version used in the dmg file name. `spctl` is still information only. It guarantees the shipped artifact is what the file name and docs say it is: the right architecture, bundle identity and version. This matters because the `Info.plist` version comes from `flutter/pubspec.yaml` (0.5.0) and the other version files say 0.5.1, so a dmg name and a bundle version that disagree could otherwise be released without anyone noticing. It is the most code and the most likely to fail on things that are expected. The version check would fail today because of the 0.5.0/0.5.1 mismatch, which the milestone explicitly only warns about and leaves unfixed. So this check has to be downgraded to a warning, or it depends on how the version-source question is settled. It also partly overlaps with the prerequisite and version-warning steps.

open-question.question: Should the script only print the dmg's SHA-256, or also write it to a sidecar file (e.g. <dmg>.sha256 in shasum format) that can be attached to the GitHub release? Which command should the user doc tell users to run to check it (shasum -a 256)?
open-question.alternative: The script prints the dmg's SHA-256 to the terminal and writes no file. The maintainer pastes the hash into the GitHub release notes. docs/macOS.md tells users to run `shasum -a 256 <dmg>` and compare the output by eye with the hash on the release page. This matches the flow in docs/Linux.md (`sha256sum` on the file, then compare with the hash listed on the official release page). This is the smallest change and matches both the Goal text ("the script prints its SHA-256") and the existing Linux guide. There is no extra artifact to upload or keep in sync, and the macOS and Linux user instructions stay parallel. The maintainer has to copy the hash into the release notes by hand, so a paste error or a stale hash can slip through. Users also have to compare 64 hex characters by eye, which is easy to get wrong and gives no clear pass/fail result.

alternative.id: Print plus shasum sidecar, compare by eye

open-question.alternative: The script prints the SHA-256 and also writes `<dmg>.sha256` next to the dmg, in the standard `shasum -a 256` output format (`<hash> <filename>`, filename only, no directory). The maintainer attaches that file to the GitHub release. docs/macOS.md still tells users to run `shasum -a 256 <dmg>` and compare the result with the published hash (from the release page or the .sha256 asset). The release gets a checksum file that machines can read, and it comes straight from the build, so no copying by hand is involved. The user doc stays as simple as the Linux guide, and users who know `shasum -c` can use it. There is one more artifact for the maintainer to upload, and it must not go stale if the dmg is rebuilt. The sidecar also only helps with transport errors: it is published by the same hand from the same place as the dmg, so anyone who can swap the dmg can swap the .sha256 too. And unless the doc shows `shasum -c`, users still compare by eye.

alternative.id: Print plus sidecar, doc uses shasum -c

open-question.alternative: The script prints the SHA-256 and writes the `<dmg>.sha256` sidecar in shasum format, with the bare filename so it checks correctly from ~/Downloads. docs/macOS.md tells users to download both files into the same directory and run `shasum -a 256 -c <dmg>.sha256`, which prints `<dmg>: OK` or FAILED. The printed hash is still shown for anyone who wants to compare by eye. Users get a clear OK/FAILED result with no manual hex comparison, which makes the "DO NOT PROCEED if it doesn't match" instruction easy to follow. The file format and the verification command are designed as a pair. Users have two downloads to manage, and the check fails confusingly if the sidecar's filename doesn't exactly match the downloaded dmg's name (for example, if the browser renamed it to "…(1).dmg"). The steps also differ from docs/Linux.md. And, as with any sidecar, it gives no protection against tampering at the release source.
